_comment: Retired copy, shared across the plugin lineage.
Keel, Better by Default and Pixel say many of the same things about the same
WordPress behaviours, so they retire the same wrong claims — and until this
file existed each kept its own list. Retiring a phrase in one repo did not
retire it in the others, which is exactly how an author-identity leak lived in
two plugins while the fix sat in the third.
Entries in `shared` are enforced by every repo that carries this file. Entries
under a repo's own key are enforced only there, because they name that
plugin's functions, options or documents and would be meaningless elsewhere.
Matching is case-insensitive substring. Keep phrases long enough to be
unambiguous and short enough to survive rewording — a phrase pinned to a whole
sentence stops matching the moment somebody improves the sentence, which is a
guard that quietly stops guarding.
A repo that explains why a phrase was retired will contain that phrase.
Better by Default is a teaching repository and does exactly that, so a bare
substring scan cannot tell a relapse from a lesson. Quote a retired phrase on
a line carrying that repo's own marker — `keel-retired-ok`,
`better-by-default-retired-ok`, `pixel-experience-retired-ok` — and the scan
skips that line. Nothing else is exempt, so the escape hatch has to be written
deliberately and is visible in review.
Matching is case-insensitive in every repo. That is not cosmetic: Better by
Default's scan was case-sensitive and its own quotation begins a sentence, so
it passed by capitalisation rather than by design, and a relapse written at the
start of a sentence would have sailed through.

shared.why: overstates an off-site link as a leak; retired in Better by Default first

shared.phrase: amplifier that batches thousands of login guesses
shared.why: the obsolete system.multicall claim — WordPress 4.4 stopped multicall being a password-guessing multiplier, so this describes a fixed vulnerability as a live one

shared.phrase: stopped testing credentials after the first failed login
shared.why: the pre-correction multicall wording; core refuses every later login in the same server instance, which is a stronger and different statement
the xmlrpc_enabled misdescription — that filter gates methods calling login(), not the endpoint, and pingback sails straight past it
concedes the argument: composition rules do enlarge the alphabet, so on paper they add entropy. What they fail to add is guessing resistance
the awkward intermediate phrasing of the same point; say 'without making them harder to guess'
